lesson.title: Beyond the Operators: Building and Editing Sets with Methods
lesson.summary: Sets support methods like .add(), .remove(), .discard(), and .update() for changing their contents in place, alongside the &, -, and ^ operators for combining sets.
lesson.body:
The Sets chapter introduced sets as unordered collections of unique elements, and the last three chapters covered the & , -, and ^ operators for combining two existing sets into a new one. Those operators are convenient, but they always produce a fresh set. Often you want to change a set that already exists, adding a new member, removing one that no longer applies, or merging in another set's contents directly. That is what set methods are for.

.add(item) inserts a single element into a set. If the element is already present, nothing happens. Duplicates are simply impossible in a set, so add() never raises an error for adding something twice, it just quietly does nothing extra. Removing elements offers two choices with an important difference: .remove(item) deletes an element but raises a KeyError if that element is not in the set, while .discard(item) removes it if present and does nothing at all if it is not. Use discard() when you are not sure the element is there and don't want your program to crash over it.

inventory = {"sword", "shield"}
inventory.add("potion")
inventory.add("sword")
inventory.discard("shield")
inventory.discard("bow")
print(sorted(inventory))

try:
    inventory.remove("bow")
except KeyError as e:
    print("KeyError:", e)

The first print shows ['potion', 'sword']: potion was added, the duplicate add of sword changed nothing, and shield was discarded. Discarding "bow", which was never in the set, caused no error. But calling remove("bow") does raise a KeyError, caught here and printed as KeyError: 'bow'.

Beyond single elements, .update(other_set) merges another set's contents directly into the existing one, acting like a mutating version of |. There are matching mutating cousins for the other operators too: .intersection_update() keeps only shared elements in place, .difference_update() removes another set's elements in place, and .symmetric_difference_update() applies ^ in place. Sets also support comparison methods worth knowing: .issubset(other) checks whether every element of a set also appears in other, .issuperset(other) checks the reverse, and .isdisjoint(other) checks whether two sets share no elements at all. Each of these returns a plain True or False, making them handy in if statements without needing to compute a whole new set first.
